items.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
items.summary:
We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies

Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.

Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org
items.t: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras

items.title: iPhone designer Tony Fadell’s next big thing: Bringing AI to fashion in hopes of saving H&M $100 million a year
items.summary:
The fashion business thrives on the conceit that it is modern, on-trend, and all about what’s happening right now . But behind the scenes—in the textile mills and garment factories that supply major brands—is an industry that runs much as it did in the 1970s. Its supply chains are splintered, chaotic, and based in warehouses that are so old-fashioned they may not even be on the internet, according to Max Easton, CEO of Smartex.AI.

Most of the work is done by hand. Checking the quality of the fabric, for instance, will be performed by a worker holding a handful of color swatches, watching a roll of cloth go by all day.

“They’re looking for simple physical defects like holes, needles, the wrong yarn, something that would be noticeable in a garment, right?” Easton said to Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon this year. For most brands, there is no such thing as a “white” T-shirt. It needs to be exactly the right shade of white—which might be a brilliant white or a creamier off-white.

But because the work is inspected by humans, fashion brands can never be quite sure that the quality of the fabric they’re buying is going to be consistent, or even match what they ordered.

“If you go to any kind of [fashion] supply chain, whether it’s fabric production or garment production, most people are just kind of amazed by how chaotic it is,” Easton said.

The chaos ends now, Smartex hopes. 

The company has been working with Tony Fadell, the legendary co-designer of the iPod, iPhone, and Nest doorbell, to launch a physical AI product that can perform fabric quality checks continuously, at…
items.t: iPhone designer Tony Fadell’s next big thing: Bringing AI to fashion in hopes of saving H&M $100 million a year

items.title: EA cofounder once compared interview questions with Amazon’s Andy Jassy—Jassy’s was so ruthless that no instant answer ends the interview
items.summary:
Amazon’s CEO Andy Jassy has one go-to interview question, and if you can’t answer it on the spot, he’ll look down at his watch and end the interview. At least, according to Bing Gordon.

Gordon was a founding exec at $55 billion EA Games—where he helped create The Sims , the game that had millennial girls around the world hooked—and Audible. He also served on Amazon’s board of directors from 2003 to 2017. 

And one time, he was sitting at dinner with fellow Amazon execs, including Jassy before he became chief exec, when the conversation turned to who had the best go-to interview question. 

“My go-to interview question is, ‘What would it take to keep you in a company like ours for 20 years? And who’s your business hero?’ And Andy Jassy had a better one,” Gordon told Fortune . “He said, ‘Mine is: what’s your strategy for constant learning?’”

Gordon instantly listed the various ways he learns, from reading books to watching people—which Jassy said was an instant green flag.

“He said: ‘Good, you know it off the top of your head. When I ask that question, if somebody goes, what do you mean? He says, as far as I’m concerned, the interview is now over, and I look at my watch and try to figure out how to get out of it.’”

Fortune reached out to Amazon for comment.

How to respond to unusual interview questions and get ahead in your 20s 

Gordon, who has just published a book, Everybody Wins , on what games and decades in Silicon Valley taught him about leadership, has some advice for getting ahead of an interviewer’s make-or-break question. “My advice to kids is, you know that…
items.t: EA cofounder once compared interview questions with Amazon’s Andy Jassy—Jassy’s was so ruthless that no instant answer ends the interview

What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors?

Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the pair were convicted of various charges deriving from what the trial judge called “the greatest financial fraud ever perpetrated in this country”. Ellison was sentenced to two years in prison after testifying against Bankman-Fried. Bankman-Fried is serving 25 years and was ordered to forfeit $11bn (£8.3bn). He says he is innocent and is applying to the supreme court to review his…

items.title: I tested an AI startup that claimed it could beat Wall Street earnings estimates. It won 40 out of 50 times
items.summary:
In 1997, a Fortune journalist observed , “The simplest, most visible, most merciless measure of corporate success…has become this one: Did you make your earnings last quarter?” Those words hold up just as well today. Indeed, the current Q3 earnings season has featured the same, decades-old ritual: Investors wait to discover if a firm can meet or exceed a consensus target from Wall Street analysts—and then reward or punish the company’s share price accordingly. Now, that ritual could be in for a shakeup.

In October, I was approached by a financial AI startup called Samaya that claimed it could predict earnings outcomes more accurately than the analysts. Prove it, I said. I invited Samaya, which raised $43 million from prominent investors in 2025, to put its money where its mouth is and provide Q3 predictions for 50 big companies, ranging from Coca-Cola to Carvana , prior to their earnings releases.

The company accepted the challenge. This led to a two-week experiment in which we placed Samaya’s AI predictions alongside the consensus view of Wall Street analysts in a spreadsheet, and then recorded the actual Q3 earnings number. Samaya didn’t just beat the analysts, it smoked them. For 40 out of the 50 companies, the AI startup’s forecasts were more accurate than the Wall Street consensus and, in most of these cases, by a considerable margin.

The experiment represents a small sample over a single earnings period, but it has potentially large implications for investors, companies and analysts alike. More broadly, the exercise underscored, once again, how AI is transforming…
items.t: I tested an AI startup that claimed it could beat Wall Street earnings estimates. It won 40 out of 50 times

items.title: ‘45 is the new 60’: Thailand’s Kasikornbank is paying staff to retire early as it prepares for AI
items.summary:
Kattiya Indaravijaya sees some similarities between what’s happening in the country’s economy and what’s going on inside Kasikornbank, the company she leads as its CEO.

For the past five years, Thailand—Southeast Asia’s second-largest economy—experienced average GDP growth of just 2.34% each year , lagging behind neighboring countries like Malaysia and Vietnam that recovered more swiftly from the pandemic.

Kattiya, CEO of Kasikornbank, believes Thailand’s inability to reinvent itself is the cause of its economic rut. “We need to restructure our economy, [because] the growth engines back then are not the growth engines now,” she tells Fortune. 

Kasikornbank is now trying to find ways to boost productivity at Thailand’s third-largest bank. “Because the economy is like this, we cannot just think about revenue generation,” Kattiya explains. “[We have to consider] cost savings too, so we’re working on a lot of productivity improvements.”

One big part of that is an early retirement scheme, named “45 is the new 60.” Employees aged 45 to 59 to apply for voluntary early retirement, and receive both standard retirement compensation and additional severance of up to a year’s salary. 

“Those who know that technology is coming in and feel that they are unable to reskill, or feel uncomfortable, they can take this package out,” Kattiya says. “We rolled this out last year, and many people took it up… so this year our [bank’s] personnel expenses are down by quite a lot.”

Thailand, too, needs to change. Kattiya explains that increasing labor costs are hindering the country’s…
items.t: ‘45 is the new 60’: Thailand’s Kasikornbank is paying staff to retire early as it prepares for AI

items.title: Why Gap has a chief entertainment officer, and why your company might need one too
items.summary:
On a warm October Saturday on Long Island, hundreds of teens packed two floors of Garden City’s Roosevelt Field mall. They were screaming, phones raised, for a boy band whose sweatshirts seemed at first glance to display the familiar GAP logo—except it spelled out J-Y-T.

This was more than product placement. JYT, short for Just Your Type, was created by longtime music producer Freddy Wexler. He pitched the group to Gap , arguing that Caden (18), Bryan (18), Tyler (17), Toby (17), and Recker (16) offered the brand the chance to build affinity with a young fan base via a capsule collection, a docuseries, and appearances at stores. “He had me at ‘mall tour,’” recalls Gap’s Pam Kaufman.

Kaufman’s title at Gap Inc. is a new one for corporate America: chief entertainment officer. In today’s fractured media market, brands are discovering that they have to do more than just collaborate with good content—they must become the content. “The most valuable real estate in culture is not a shelf, an ad, a storefront, or an Instagram post,” Kaufman says. “It’s attention.” With competition for customers’ time just a scroll away, the only way to guarantee eyeballs (and wallets) is to make something they can’t look away from. That’s Kaufman’s mandate in this new C-suite role, one other brands may soon be casting for themselves.

The chief entertainment officer role was dreamed up by Gap Inc. CEO Richard Dickson , who joined the $15-billion-in-revenue parent of Old Navy, Banana Republic, Athleta, and the Gap apparel chain in 2023 from Mattel . There, he had turned the Barbie doll into a…
items.t: Why Gap has a chief entertainment officer, and why your company might need one too

items.title: Sunrun and Overview Energy CEOs say the answer to AI’s energy problem is already on the grid
items.summary:
AI has an energy problem. Two solar executives at opposite ends of the industry believe much of the answer lies in flexibility, and in getting more out of the power plants, power lines, and batteries the country already has.

“We need more generation, that’s true, but we already have all these assets on the grid that we’re just not taking advantage of,” said Abdullah Al-Shakarchi, co-CEO of Overview Energy, onstage at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit this week. “Gas plants are 60, 70% utilized based on where you are. Transmission often sits doing nothing. And so what are the right solutions that we can build to take advantage of what we’ve already got? Because that lets us lower the amount of things that we need to build. And I think that is the future of energy.”

Sunrun CEO Mary Powell, whose company installs rooftop solar and home batteries, agreed. “Ultimately, it is about having power generated right where it’s needed,” she said in the session, moderated by Fortune ‘s Allie Garfinkle. “I mean, the grid was constructed as it is over 100 years ago. And it’s just time that we really advance it.”

Sunrun had about 1.06 million subscribers and 5 gigawatt-hours of networked home battery storage as of Sept. 30, according to its third-quarter results . “We sit on top of right now gigawatt-hours of energy,” Powell said. “Some of it’s being used by the grid, but I really see the next couple of years as an opportunity to crack that wide open and have all of those resources used in a way that can then make the grid more financially viable for everybody.”

The push for…
items.t: Sunrun and Overview Energy CEOs say the answer to AI’s energy problem is already on the grid

The largest partnership agreed Wednesday, valued at approximately $50 billion, hopes to foster 10 “future smart cities”; the agreement links an arm of Danantara, Indonesia’s sovereign wealth fund, with a consortium led by China’s Shaanxi Construction Engineering Group.

“That will ​become a historic project to be implemented next year,” said Rosan Roeslani, Indonesia’s minister of investment and downstream industry and Danantara’s chief executive officer. He added that the investments will “have a positive impact on job creation and will also facilitate technology transfer.”

Danantara said earlier this month that it plans to develop a dozen smart cities, envisioned as integrated urban areas combining residential communities, universities, hospitals, shopping centers, and infrastructure.

A second agreement pairs Danantara with Hisense, the Chinese appliance maker, on a $10 billion investment in technology and manufacturing, including new research labs and manufacturing facilities for household appliances. items.title: If Indonesia wants 8% growth, it needs to give investors confidence that contracts won’t change on them
items.summary:
Indonesia faces a test of investor confidence. A volatile stretch for the stock market, pressure on the rupiah, and concerns over fiscal discipline and policy uncertainty have raised questions about the direction of Southeast Asia’s largest economy—questions sharpened by MSCI’s proposal to reclassify Indonesian equities to “standalone” status, outside the benchmark emerging-market indexes that guide global portfolios.

Yet despite these wobbles, the long-term investment case for Indonesia remains strong. I saw it firsthand in Jakarta, where I recently led a business delegation of 33 American companies—investors, employers, and partners in developing Indonesia’s workforce. Across engagements with senior government officials and business leaders, one takeaway was clear: The U.S. business community remains committed to the Indonesian market.

But confidence cannot be taken for granted.

President Prabowo Subianto has set an ambitious target of 8% economic growth by 2029. Indonesia’s economy expanded 5.47% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, and the government is targeting 6% growth in 2027. Indonesia has the resources, talent, and market to pursue these ambitions. The challenge is creating the conditions that turn that potential into sustained investment.

Our discussions reinforced a simple point: Indonesia’s next wave of investment need not come only from new entrants. It can come from companies already operating there—businesses that have built factories, developed suppliers, trained workers, and established deep roots in the economy.

items.t: If Indonesia wants 8% growth, it needs to give investors confidence that contracts won’t change on them

Anthropic’s stock will begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker ANT, marking one of the most highly anticipated IPOs in years as well as one of the largest ever. 

The San Francisco-based AI company said Wednesday that it increased the number of shares sold in the offering to 980 million, instead of the 825 million shares it initially indicated it would sell. The expanded float means Anthropic will raise roughly $79.4 billion in the IPO—and as much as $91.6 billion if the deal’s underwriters choose to exercise an over-allotment option.

The IPO will also make instant billionaires out of numerous Anthropic employees and early investors, particularly the seven cofounders who created Anthropic in San Francisco just five years ago. Some—including CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniella Amodei, and Chief Science Officer Jared Kaplan—are cashing in small portions of their equity through the offering, with existing shareholders selling 23.6 million shares.

At a $1.5 trillion valuation, Anthropic would be the second most valuable IPO of all time, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO in June. Measured by capital raised however, Anthropic’s $79 billion would top the $75 billon raised by SpaceX.

The offering will provide Anthropic with a vital infusion of capital as it seeks to stay ahead in the AI race and to invest in the computing infrastructure to train its models. Seven…

items.title: ‘A failure of implementation’: AI played a key role in some outages—but not in the way you might think
items.summary:
Many people are understandably shaken after a string of nationwide outages over the past week—from flights being grounded, to emails not coming through, bank transactions failing, and much more—with no clear explanation from politicians or businesses about what exactly happened.

One thing officials have made clear is that the outages are not a result of a coordinated cyberattack, quelling fears that AI may have empowered bad actors to take down critical systems. However, AI still appears to have played a significant, if unexpected, role. Advanced AI models are speeding up the discovery of software vulnerabilities, which tech teams are racing to patch before bad actors can exploit them with equally powerful AI tools. 

The botched implementation of those patches was linked to an outage earlier this week of an internal communications system at the National Security Agency (NSA), as well as the “banking outages,” a spokesperson for Senator Mark Warner’s team told Fortune . Bank of America , Wells Fargo , and JPMorgan Chase all suffered outages this week.

“It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said in a statement. The Washington Sun also reported that bank CEOs and the NSA told Congress that AI-driven patches were to blame for the service disruptions.

The irony is that the tools aimed at preventing system outages seem to be causing them, or at least influencing new forms of human error. Bank of America disclosed last month it had hired 1,000 contractors to patch flaws exposed by…
items.t: ‘A failure of implementation’: AI played a key role in some outages—but not in the way you might think

items.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
items.summary:
He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
items.summary:
It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year

  • Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166

The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January. But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving.

Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use.

Continue reading...
items.t: Energy price cap rise: how to beat the January hike

items.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
items.summary:
After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs

When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI.

But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

Continue reading...
items.t: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte

items.title: David Beckham's perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink | Arwa Mahdawi
items.summary:
The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares

Thoughts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while, and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down.

Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire. I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company, Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m).

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.
